Assume a straight rectangular beam with constant width b and height h and with coordinate x along the beam axis, y measured from the centroidal neutral axis in the bending plane, and z along the neutral bending axis.
Assume the material is homogeneous, isotropic, and linear elastic with Young's modulus E.
Assume small deformations and Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, so plane sections remain plane and the neutral axis passes through the centroid of the rectangular cross section.
Let M(x) be the internal bending moment at section x, taken positive about the z-axis according to the chosen sign convention.
The bending strain at a fiber with coordinate y is epsilon_x(x,y) = -M(x) y / (E I_z).
The bending stress at that fiber is sigma_x(x,y) = E epsilon_x(x,y) = -M(x) y / I_z.
The area moment of inertia of the rectangular cross section is I_z = b h^3 / 12.
The maximum bending stress magnitude occurs at the outermost fibers y = plus or minus h/2 and is |sigma_max| = |M(x)| h / (2 I_z) = 6 |M(x)| / (b h^2).
The curvature is kappa(x) = M(x) / (E I_z).
If an axial force N is present, add the uniform axial stress N/(b h) to sigma_x.
If a transverse shear force V(x) is present, the shear stress distribution is tau_xy(x,y) = V(x) Q(y) / (I_z b), with Q(y) = (b/2)(h^2/4 - y^2).
These bending stress relations are valid away from load application points and supports by Saint-Venant's principle.
